warmup.q: The counting program reads the chain's payments from Kafka and counts how many it reads in each second. The cafés take a steady 100 payments a second. The program is stopped for 60 seconds, and Kafka keeps the payments that arrive meanwhile. When it starts again, it reads that backlog as fast as it can, 2,000 payments a second. What does the chart show for the first second after the restart?
options: 100: each payment carries the time it was made
About 2,000: it counts what it read in that second
0: those payments belong to the minute that has already passed
About 6,000: the whole backlog at once
warmup.why: The chart counts the payments the program read in each second, so it shows how fast the program reads, not how fast people pay. For three seconds that's 2,000, twenty times the real rate, after a minute of zeros. Each payment does carry the time it was made (the first option), but that only helps if the chart groups payments by that time, which the first section does. The backlog of 6,000 takes three seconds to read, not one, because the program's top speed is 2,000 a second.

sections.h: A restart invents a spike: event time and processing time
sections.html:
Let's build the counting program from the opening. Each time a card is tapped at one of the chain's tills, the payments app writes a small record to Kafka. It says which card, which shop, how much, and the time of the tap. A record of something that happened is called an event, and a flow of events that never ends is a stream. Kafka keeps each stream as a topic, a named log that programs add events to and read from in order. A program that reads a topic is called a consumer.

Our consumer counts the chain's payments per second for the chart. The numbers in this lesson are made up for teaching. The cafés take a steady 100 payments a second, and each one takes 5 ms (thousandths of a second) to get from the till to the consumer. The obvious way to count is to look at the consumer's own clock as each payment arrives, and add one to that second's count.

Now stop the consumer to install a new version and start it again, which is called a redeploy. The old version stops at 60 s and the new one starts at 120 s. Kafka keeps every event for days, read or not, so the 6,000 payments made in between wait there. The new consumer reads that backlog as fast as it can, 2,000 a second. Here's the chart, second by second: 100, then zero for a whole minute, then 2,000, 2,000, 2,000, 400, and back to 100.

That's a spike twenty times the real rate, after a dip that never happened either. An alarm set at five times normal goes off. A rule that blocks a shop at more than 1,000 payments a second, a cheap guard against stolen cards, blocks the whole chain.

The chart mixed up two clocks. Event time is when the thing happened: the till stamped the time of the tap into the event. Processing time is when our code reads the event, by the consumer's own clock. On a quiet day the two are a few milliseconds apart, so mixing them up costs nothing. They come apart whenever events wait somewhere. A redeploy makes them wait. So does a slow network link, or a Kafka computer that fails and hands its work to another. So does a job that reads last week's events again, or a phone that was offline for an hour and sends its taps all at once.

The post works the same way. A friend on holiday sends you one postcard a day. The post office closes for a week, then delivers all seven cards on one morning. Count by the day each card lands in your letterbox, and your friend wrote nothing for a week, then seven cards in one day. The postmark tells the truth. The postmark is the event time, and the day a card lands is the processing time.

So counting by processing time measured the consumer, not the cafés. Count the same events by the time stamped in each one, and every second shows 100 (the Try it prints both). Batch jobs, programs that work through a big pile of old records in one run, always worked this way. A job that reads last year's payments groups them by the times written in the data, because its own clock only says "today".

Event time has two costs. The first is trust. The timestamp comes from the till's clock, and Clocks you can't trust showed how far such clocks drift; a phone's clock can be hours off. Phone apps that save events while offline record three times: when it happened on the phone, when the phone sent it, and when the company's computers received it. The gap between the last two shows how wrong the phone's clock is, and the app corrects the first time by that much.

The second cost shapes the rest of this lesson. By processing time, the count for 10:01:07 is final the moment the clock passes 10:01:08. By event time, the clock tells you nothing. A payment made at 10:01:07 can arrive a minute later, after a redeploy. It can even arrive after a payment from 10:01:08 that came along a faster path, the way Tuesday's postcard can turn up after Wednesday's. So when is the count for a second final? First we need to say which second, or which minute, each payment counts in.

try.title: Count one redeploy both ways
steps: From the labs folder, run SpikeDemo (command below). It's plain Kotlin on a pretend clock that the program moves forward itself, so it finishes in a moment. It makes 100 payments a second for 3 minutes, with the consumer stopped from 60 s to 120 s.
Before it prints, predict the counts by processing time for seconds 120 to 123.

code.title: SpikeDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l04.demo /** * Lesson stream-04, Try it 1: a fraud dashboard counts card authorizations per second for one * merchant. 100 a second arrive, steadily. The counting consumer is redeployed: it stops at 60 s and * starts again at 120 s, then drains Kafka's backlog at 2,000 a second. Count the same events by * processing time and by event time. */ /** (event time, processing time) in ms for every event, in the order the consumer read them. */ fun redeploy(perSecond: Int = 100, seconds: Int = 180, stopAt: Long = 60_000, restartAt: Long = 120_000, drainPerSecond: Int = 2_000): List<Pair<Long, Long>> { val spacingUs = 1_000_000L / drainPerSecond var freeAtUs = 0L return (0 until perSecond * seconds).map { i -> val eventTime = i * 1000L / perSecond var readyUs = (eventTime + 5) * 1000 // 5 ms from the card terminal to the consumer if (readyUs >= stopAt * 1000 && readyUs < restartAt * 1000) readyUs = restartAt * 1000 // waits in Kafka val startUs = maxOf(readyUs, freeAtUs) freeAtUs = startUs + spacingUs eventTime to startUs / 1000 } } fun main() { val events = redeploy() val byProcessing = events.groupingBy { it.second / 1000 }.eachCount() val byEvent = events.groupingBy { it.first / 1000 }.eachCount() println("second | by processing time | by event time") for (s in listOf(58L, 59, 60, 61, 119, 120, 121, 122, 123, 124, 125)) { println("%6d | %18d | %13d".format(s, byProcessing[s] ?: 0, byEvent[s] ?: 0)) } println("max per second: by processing time ${byProcessing.values.max()}, by event time ${byEvent.values.max()}") println("seconds with zero by processing time: ${(0L until 180).count { byProcessing[it] == null }}") }

sections.h: Windows cut an endless stream into pieces you can count
sections.html:
The chart from the first section counts per second, and a rule against stolen cards might count per five minutes. Either way, a count needs a start and an end, and a stream has neither. "Payments per minute" only means something once we say which minutes. A window is a stretch of event time with a start and an end, such as 09:10 to 09:15. The program puts each event into one or more windows by its event time, and keeps a count for each window. There are four kinds you'll meet, and the figure shows where each kind puts three payments made with one card.

The plainest kind is the tumbling window. Tumbling windows all have the same size, sit end to end with no overlap, and line up with the clock. Five-minute windows run 09:10 to 09:15, 09:15 to 09:20, and so on. A window includes its start and leaves out its end, so a payment at exactly 09:15:00.000 belongs to the second one. Every event lands in exactly one window. Use them for "payments per minute".

Tumbling windows have a blind spot. Picture a rule against stolen cards: "three payments on one card within 5 minutes". A thief taps a stolen card at 09:14:20 and again at 09:16:10, under 2 minutes apart. Yet the two taps fall in different tumbling windows, so neither window sees both.

Hopping windows are the first fix. They have a fixed size too, but a new one starts at a fixed step called the advance: say a 5-minute window starting every minute. They overlap, so each event lands in size ÷ advance windows, 5 here, and the two taps share some of them. Use hopping windows for "the last 5 minutes, updated every minute". They cost 5 times the counts and 5 times the results.

Sliding windows come from the events instead of the clock. Two events share a window if they're at most 5 minutes apart, wherever the clock's minute marks fall. Kafka Streams, a library for writing stream programs in Java that the next lesson opens up, makes one sliding window per event. It runs from 5 minutes before the event up to the event, and includes both ends.

Session windows have no fixed size at all. They're kept per key, the value that events are grouped by, such as the card. A session goes on while events keep coming, and ends after a gap with none, say 30 minutes. In postcard terms, a session is "every card from one trip", however long the trip was. A late event that lands in a gap can join two sessions into one, so a session counter must be able to merge windows (the lab does this).

Watch the names. Kafka Streams calls the fixed-size, overlapping kind hopping (TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(size).advanceBy(advance)), and saves "sliding" for the one-window-per-event kind (SlidingWindows). Flink, a program that runs stream programs across many computers, and Apache Beam, a way of writing stream programs for such engines, do it the other way. They follow Google's Dataflow model, from a 2015 research paper, and call the fixed-size overlapping kind sliding. When someone says "sliding window", ask which one they mean.

The kinds also differ in what they must remember. What a program remembers between events is called its state. A tumbling count keeps one number per key for each window that can still change. Hopping keeps one per overlapping window, five times as many here. Sliding and session windows have to keep the events themselves, or partial sums, for every window that might still change. The next lesson, Kafka Streams: tables, state and windows, builds these in a real engine.

Windows tell us where an event counts. They don't tell us when a window is done, and that's the next question.

try.title: Put four payments into windows
steps: Run WindowsDemo (command below). It takes four payments on one card, at 09:10:30, 09:14:20, 09:16:10 and 09:52:00, and prints the windows each kind puts them in.
Predict first: which tumbling windows split two payments that are less than 5 minutes apart? And how many sessions does a 30-minute gap give?

code.title: WindowsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l04.demo /** * Lesson stream-04, Try it 2: four card authorizations by one customer, and the windows each kind * of window puts them in. Times are hh:mm:ss on one day. */ fun hms(ms: Long) = "%02d:%02d:%02d".format(ms / 3_600_000, ms / 60_000 % 60, ms / 1000 % 60) fun at(h: Int, m: Int, s: Int) = (h * 3600L + m * 60L + s) * 1000 fun span(start: Long, end: Long) = "[${hms(start)}, ${hms(end)})" fun main() { val minute = 60_000L val times = listOf(at(9, 10, 30), at(9, 14, 20), at(9, 16, 10), at(9, 52, 0)) println("tumbling, 5 minutes (aligned to 00:00:00, start included, end excluded):") for (t in times) { val s = t - t % (5 * minute); println(" ${hms(t)} -> ${span(s, s + 5 * minute)}") } println("hopping, 5 minutes, advancing by 1 minute (Flink and Beam call this sliding):") val t = times[1] val windows = generateSequence(t - t % minute) { it - minute }.takeWhile { it + 5 * minute > t }.toList().reversed() println(" ${hms(t)} is in ${windows.size} windows: ${windows.joinToString(" ") { span(it, it + 5 * minute) }}") println("sliding, 5 minutes (Kafka Streams: one window per record, both ends included):") for (end in times) { val inside = times.filter { it in (end - 5 * minute)..end } println(" [${hms(end - 5 * minute)}, ${hms(end)}] holds ${inside.size}: ${inside.joinToString { hms(it) }}") } println("session, 30-minute inactivity gap:") val sessions = mutableListOf(mutableListOf(times[0])) for (x in times.drop(1)) if (x - sessions.last().last() <= 30 * minute) sessions.last() += x else sessions += mutableListOf(x) sessions.forEach { println(" ${hms(it.first())} to ${hms(it.last())}: ${it.size} event${if (it.size == 1) "" else "s"}") } }

sections.h: A watermark says when a window is complete enough
sections.html:
Back to the question from the first section: when is the window 10:00 to 10:01 complete? The simplest answer uses processing time again. Wait until the consumer's clock passes 10:01, add 10 seconds for stragglers, and send out the count. A straggler is an event that arrives later than its neighbours, like Tuesday's postcard after Wednesday's.

That breaks at the first redeploy. After a 60-second stop, every window of that minute closes the moment the consumer comes back, before it has read a single event of its backlog. The counts come out as zeros, and the real payments arrive to find their windows gone.

So measure progress in event time instead. A watermark is a claim the program keeps up to date: "I believe no more events with an event time earlier than W will arrive." When the watermark passes a window's end, the window is closed and its result goes out. Sending a result on, to the chart or to an alarm, is called emitting it.

The simplest watermark is the largest event time seen so far, minus an allowance for disorder. With your postcards, it's the latest postmark you've received, minus a few days for slow post. Once that passes the end of July, you add up July.

Each engine has its own version. Kafka splits each topic into partitions, separate logs that different computers can read side by side, and events stay in order only within one partition. Flink keeps a watermark like ours for each partition it reads. A step that reads several partitions takes the smallest of their watermarks, since it can only be as sure as its least sure input. Spark, another engine, uses the largest event time seen minus a delay you choose (lesson 8 of this track). Kafka Streams has no separate watermark. It splits its work into tasks, one per partition, and each task tracks its stream time, the largest timestamp it has seen. Then you give each window a grace period, a stretch of extra waiting. This lesson's stepper and lab use that model.

A watermark is a guess, and the Dataflow paper (Akidau and others, 2015) names its two ways of failing.

  • Too fast: an event older than the watermark still arrives, from a phone that was offline or a partition that fell behind the others. That's a late event, and the next section deals with it.
  • Too slow: a watermark that takes the smallest over its inputs waits for the slowest one. One partition that receives nothing, or one stuck till, holds every window open, and results come late or never. Flink lets you mark an input that has gone quiet as idle, so it stops holding the watermark back.

The same paper frames the whole problem as four questions. What are you computing (a count)? Where in event time (which windows)? When in processing time do you emit results (watermarks, and the triggers of the next section)? And how do later results relate to earlier ones? Its starting point is to stop pretending you'll ever know you've seen everything, and to build for corrections instead.

The stepper runs a watermark over one payment a second with three stragglers, and the Try it lets you change the grace period. Watch the stragglers that arrive after their window has closed: those are the next section's problem.

frames.say: The watermark is a guess about completeness, and it can be wrong both ways. Too fast: events older than it still arrive, as here. try.title: Close windows with a watermark, then add grace
steps: Run WatermarkDemo (command below) with no grace. It prints each window as it becomes final, and each straggler as it arrives.
Run it again with 10 seconds of grace (-Pargs=10), then with 60 (-Pargs=60). Before each run, predict how many stragglers are dropped, and when the first window becomes final.

code.title: WatermarkDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l04.demo /** * Lesson stream-04, Try it 3: one-minute counts for merchant m-7 with a watermark. One on-time event * a second (event times 0 s to 299 s) and three stragglers that arrive after the stream has passed * the end of their window by 5 s, 30 s and 90 s. Run it with a grace period: -Pargs=10 (seconds). */ data class Ev(val eventTime: Long, val note: String = "") fun stragglers(): List<Ev> = buildList { for (s in 0 until 300) { add(Ev(s * 1000L)) when (s) { 65 -> add(Ev(59_000, "late: 5 s past its window")) 150 -> add(Ev(100_000, "late: 30 s past its window")) 270 -> add(Ev(130_000, "late: 90 s past its window")) } } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val grace = (args.firstOrNull()?.toLong() ?: 0) * 1000 val size = 60_000L var watermark = Long.MIN_VALUE // stream time: the largest event time seen so far val open = sortedMapOf<Long, Int>() // window start -> count var dropped = 0 println("1-minute windows, grace ${grace / 1000} s") for (e in stragglers()) { watermark = maxOf(watermark, e.eventTime) val start = e.eventTime - e.eventTime % size if (start + size + grace <= watermark) { dropped++ println(" watermark %3d s: event at %3d s DROPPED, window %3d-%3d s already closed (${e.note})".format(watermark / 1000, e.eventTime / 1000, start / 1000, (start + size) / 1000)) continue } if (e.note.isNotEmpty()) println(" watermark %3d s: event at %3d s counted, window %3d-%3d s still open (${e.note})".format(watermark / 1000, e.eventTime / 1000, start / 1000, (start + size) / 1000)) open.merge(start, 1, Int::plus) while (open.isNotEmpty() && open.firstKey() + size + grace <= watermark) { val s = open.firstKey() println(" watermark %3d s: window %3d-%3d s is final, count = %d".format(watermark / 1000, s / 1000, (s + size) / 1000, open.remove(s))) } } println(" end of input: still open ${open.keys.map { "${it / 1000}-${(it + size) / 1000} s" }}") println("dropped as late: $dropped") }

try.expect:
1-minute windows, grace 0 s
  watermark  60 s: window   0- 60 s is final, count = 60
  watermark  65 s: event at  59 s DROPPED, window   0- 60 s already closed (late: 5 s past its window)
  watermark 120 s: window  60-120 s is final, count = 60
  watermark 150 s: event at 100 s DROPPED, window  60-120 s already closed (late: 30 s past its window)
  watermark 180 s: window 120-180 s is final, count = 60
  watermark 240 s: window 180-240 s is final, count = 60
  watermark 270 s: event at 130 s DROPPED, window 120-180 s already closed (late: 90 s past its window)
  end of input: still open [240-300 s]
dropped as late: 3

With -Pargs=10, the first straggler is counted (its window closes at 70 s with 61) and two are dropped. With -Pargs=60, the first window waits until the watermark reaches 120 s and closes with 61, the second also closes with 61, and only the payment 90 s past its window is dropped. More grace keeps more stragglers, and delays every result by the same amount.

refs.title: Akidau et al.: The Dataflow Model (watermarks, triggers, accumulation)

aside.title: Why can't each till say when it's done?
aside.html: They can, in a way. Each till could send a marker now and then that says "nothing older than 10:01 will come from me". The counter would then wait until every till had sent one. But it would have to know every till, and the chain adds and removes tills all the time. One till with a dead battery would hold every window open for good. A watermark is a guess made from the events themselves, so it keeps working when tills come and go.

video.title: A watermark closes a window, and a late event is dropped

sections.h: What to do with a late event: drop it, wait for it, or correct the answer
sections.html:
The last Try it had three stragglers. Each arrived after the watermark had passed the end of its window: one by 5 seconds, one by 30 and one by 90. An event like that is called late. Unless something keeps its window open, the window's count has already gone out. You can do three things with a late event, and most programs combine them.

The cheapest is to drop it and count the drop, and most engines do this unless told otherwise. Kafka Streams skips late events and counts them in a metric, a number the program reports about itself; this one is dropped-records-total. Flink can send them to a side output instead, a second stream where a slower program fixes the totals later. Whatever the engine, set an alarm on that count. A rising number of late events means one till, or one partition, is in trouble.

The second is to wait a little longer, with a grace period. Kafka Streams calls it grace (TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(10))), and Flink calls it allowed lateness, 0 unless you set it. The window stays open that much longer after the watermark passes its end. The lab's three stragglers arrive 5 s, 30 s and 90 s after their windows ended. A grace of 0 drops all three, 10 s drops two, and 60 s drops one. The price is time and memory. With 60 s of grace, the count for 10:00 to 10:01 comes out at 10:02, and every window is remembered a minute longer.

A grace of 0 looks fine in tests, where events arrive in order. With real traffic, every hiccup delivers a few events after the watermark has moved on, and each one quietly goes missing from the totals.

The third is to answer early and correct later. A trigger is the rule for when a window emits a result, which can differ from when it closes. A rule against stolen cards can't wait for the watermark plus grace. So its window emits early, say every minute by the program's clock, then again when the watermark passes, and once more for each late event inside the grace period. Now one window gives several results, and whatever receives them, the sink, has to know how they relate. The Dataflow model names three ways, called accumulation modes:

  • Discarding: each result holds only the events since the last one (14, 11, 9, and so on), and the sink must add them up.
  • Accumulating: each result holds the total so far (14, 25, 34, and so on), and the sink must replace the previous value for that window. A sink that adds them instead counts 232 events where there were 57 (the Try it shows it).
  • Accumulating and retracting: each result says "take back 25, add 34". You need this when another step groups the results again, say summing each shop's counts into a count per city. Without the "take back", that step can't undo a number it already added.

Back to the postcards: a friend who phones each evening with the trip's total so far ("12 cards now") is accumulating. One who texts only the new cards ("3 more today") is discarding.

Kafka Streams emits an updated count for every event, unless told otherwise: a stream of running totals that the sink must treat as replacements. suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(unbounded())) turns that into one final result per window. The next lesson builds both.

Pick by what a wrong answer costs. The stolen-card rule wants a fast early number and can live with a correction. Paying each shop what it took that day needs the final number. That job waits out the grace period, and a batch job that reads the whole day again at night fixes any later stragglers.

A stream has no last event, so every final count is a choice of how long to wait. Choose it, and count what you drop.

That choice is the limit of everything in this lesson: a longer wait gives more complete answers and later ones, and no setting gives you both. Every open window also has to live somewhere while it waits, and that's where the next lesson starts.

try.title: One window, six results, three accumulation modes
steps: Run TriggerDemo (command below). The window 10:00 to 10:05 fires early every minute, on time when the watermark passes 10:05, and once more for a late event inside the grace period.
Predict: in accumulating mode, what total does a sink end with if it adds up every result it receives?

code.title: TriggerDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.stream.l04.demo /** * Lesson stream-04, Try it 4: the fraud team wants a count for the 10:00-10:05 window early, not * 5 minutes plus grace later. The window fires early every minute of processing time, fires again * when the watermark passes its end, and once more for each late event inside the grace period. * What each firing sends downstream depends on the accumulation mode. */ data class Firing(val at: String, val why: String, val newEvents: Int) fun main() { // what the window had seen at each firing (events that arrived since the previous firing) val firings = listOf( Firing("10:01", "early (1 min of processing time)", 14), Firing("10:02", "early", 11), Firing("10:03", "early", 9), Firing("10:04", "early", 12), Firing("10:05", "on time: the watermark passed 10:05", 10), Firing("10:06", "late event, inside the grace period", 1), ) println("%-6s %-38s %10s %13s %s".format("fires", "why", "discarding", "accumulating", "accumulating and retracting")) var total = 0 for (f in firings) { val before = total total += f.newEvents val retracting = if (before == 0) "+$total" else "-$before, +$total" println("%-6s %-38s %10d %13d %s".format(f.at, f.why, f.newEvents, total, retracting)) } println() println("a sink that adds up what it receives gets the right total from discarding: ${firings.sumOf { it.newEvents }}") println("a sink that adds up accumulating panes counts the same events again: ${firings.runningFold(0) { a, f -> a + f.newEvents }.drop(1).sum()}") println("a sink that upserts by window keeps the last accumulating pane: $total") }

try.expect:
fires  why                                    discarding  accumulating  accumulating and retracting
10:01  early (1 min of processing time)               14            14  +14
10:02  early                                          11            25  -14, +25
10:03  early                                           9            34  -25, +34
10:04  early                                          12            46  -34, +46
10:05  on time: the watermark passed 10:05            10            56  -46, +56
10:06  late event, inside the grace period             1            57  -56, +57

a sink that adds up what it receives gets the right total from discarding: 57
a sink that adds up accumulating panes counts the same events again: 232
a sink that upserts by window keeps the last accumulating pane: 57

The same six firings mean different things in each mode. Discarding results add up to 57. Accumulating results are running totals, so a sink that adds them reports 232 for 57 events; it must replace the value for the window instead. Retracting results carry both the value to take back and the new one, which is what a second counting step needs.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 Streams DSL: grace periods and suppress

opening:
Picture the company that records card payments for a big café chain. Each tap of a card goes into Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages for other programs to read. One program counts the payments per second for a chart: about 100 a second.

One morning, the counting program stops for a minute while a new version goes in. Back again, its chart shows a minute of zeros, then three seconds at 2,000 a second. An alarm goes off, and a rule against stolen cards blocks the whole chain. At the cafés, nothing changed.

It's easy to count by the program's own clock: it's right there, and on a normal day it agrees with the tills.

In Event sourcing and CQRS, we rebuilt answers by replaying a log, a month of payments in minutes. Replays are where a program's clock is most wrong. In this lesson, we'll count the same payments by two clocks, cut them into windows, and decide when a count is final. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a chart that showed a minute of zeros and then a spike, while the cafés took 100 payments a second throughout. It counted by the clock of the program reading the payments. Counting by the time stamped in each payment fixes that, and leaves one choice: how long to wait before a count is final.

Find a card statement, on paper or in your bank's app. Many show two dates for each payment: the day you paid and the day the bank recorded it. Which one decides the month a payment counts in?

Next, we'll build these windows in Kafka Streams, and find out where its counts live and how they come back after a lost disk.

compare.title: Counting per minute by processing time and by event time

a.label: Processing time
a.title: bucket by the consumer's clock
a.html: for (record in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { val minute = System.currentTimeMillis() / 60_000 // when WE read it counts.merge(record.key() to minute, 1, Int::plus) } // a minute is final when the clock passes it: simple, and wrong after every redeploy

b.label: Event time
b.title: bucket by the event's timestamp, close by watermark
b.html: for (record in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { val t = record.value().authorizedAt // when it HAPPENED watermark = maxOf(watermark, t) val window = t - t % 60_000 if (window + 60_000 + grace <= watermark) { lateDropped++; continue } counts.merge(record.key() to window, 1, Int::plus) emitWindowsEndingBefore(watermark - grace) // final counts, once }

compare.note: The left side needs nothing but the current minute, and its counts are final at once, but it measures the consumer: a backlog becomes a spike. The right side measures the cafés. In return it keeps several windows open, needs a grace period, and has to decide what to do with events that come after it. The watermark here is the largest event time seen, as in Kafka Streams; Flink would also subtract an allowance for disorder and take the smallest across partitions.

worked.title: Design a stolen-card check that counts payments per shop

steps.say: The code is Kafka Streams, which the next lesson explains call by call. What: count payments per shop. Where in event time: 5-minute windows that move forward every minute (hopping), grouped by shop, on the time the till stamped into each payment.
steps.code: val windows = TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5), Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .advanceBy(Duration.ofMinutes(1)) // hopping: 5 windows per event

steps.say: Measure how late your events really are before you pick the grace, over a normal day and over a redeploy. Kafka Streams reports it per task as record-lateness-avg and record-lateness-max: stream time minus the event's own time. Suppose 999 payments in 1,000 arrive within 12 s, and a redeploy adds up to 20 s more. Then 30 s of grace covers both (made-up numbers).
steps.code: // what record-lateness measures, if you track it yourself in a plain consumer streamTime = maxOf(streamTime, event.authorizedAt) latenessHistogram.record(streamTime - event.authorizedAt)

steps.say: When in processing time: the check can't wait 5 minutes plus grace, so it uses every update as it comes (an early trigger). It treats each one as the running total for its window, and never adds them up.
steps.code: builder.stream<String, Authorization>("authorizations") .groupByKey() .windowedBy(windows) .count() // emits an updated total per record: accumulating .toStream() .filter { _, n -> n > 1_000 }

steps.say: How later results relate to earlier ones: the chart stores each update under (shop, window start), so a later total replaces an earlier one. The nightly payout to each shop instead waits until the window closes, and gets exactly one number per window.
steps.code: .suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(Suppressed.BufferConfig.unbounded())) // one final count per window

steps.say: Watch what falls off the end. Set an alarm on the count of dropped late events for each task. If it rises after a redeploy, check how far behind the partitions are before you raise the grace period.
steps.code: # an alarm rule: fire if any late events were dropped in the last 5 minutes. # The metric is dropped-records-total; its exact name depends on your monitoring tool. rate(kafka_streams_task_dropped_records_total[5m]) > 0

lab.title: Windows, a watermark and late events on a pretend clock
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code. All 16 fail. They need no Docker: Streams.kt (given) builds three scenarios on a pretend clock: the redeploy, three stragglers, and 6,000 events that each take up to 2 s to arrive.

In Windows.kt, write tumbling (round the time down to a multiple of the size) and hopping (every window that starts at a multiple of the advance and still contains the time). The redeploy tests then show the 20x spike by processing time and a flat 100 by event time.
Write sessions: sort the times, and start a new session wherever the gap to the previous event is more than the gap allowed.

In WindowedCounter.kt, write onEvent and flush. onEvent raises the watermark, drops the event if its window has closed, counts it, and then closes every window whose end plus grace is at or below the watermark. Run the tests until all 16 pass, and look at how the number of drops changes with the grace period.
hints: A window is closed when end + graceMs <= watermark. Check it after you raise the watermark with this event.
Keep the open counts in a TreeMap keyed by (window start, key), so the earliest windows close first.
hopping: start at t - t % advanceMs, step back by advanceMs while the window still reaches past t and its start is at least 0, then reverse the list.

drill.title: A watermark counter from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write the step that a tumbling-window counter runs for each event. It uses the largest event time seen as its watermark, and it has a grace period. Then answer: with 1-minute windows and 10 s of grace, is an event with event time 59 s counted if it arrives when the watermark is 69 s? And if it arrives when the watermark is already 70 s?

answer.html: fun onEvent(e: Event) { watermark = maxOf(watermark, e.eventTime) val start = e.eventTime - e.eventTime % size if (start + size + grace <= watermark) { // its window already closed lateDropped++ return } open.merge(start to e.key, 1, Int::plus) while (open.isNotEmpty() && open.firstKey().first + size + grace <= watermark) { val (k, count) = open.pollFirstEntry() emit(k.second, k.first, count) // final, once } } // event at 59 s, watermark 69 s: window 0-60 closes at 60 + 10 = 70 > 69, so it is counted. // watermark 70 s: 70 >= 70, the window is closed and its count already emitted: dropped as late.

recap: Event time is when something happened, stamped in the event. Processing time is when your code reads it. Counting by processing time measures the reader: a 60-second redeploy becomes a minute of zeros and a spike 20 times the real rate.

Windows make a stream countable: tumbling (fixed size, no overlap), hopping (fixed size, overlapping), sliding (built from events that are close together) and session (ends after a quiet gap). Kafka Streams' "hopping" is what Flink and Beam call "sliding".

A watermark claims that no earlier events will still arrive. When it passes a window's end, plus any grace period, the window's result is final. Kafka Streams uses stream time, the largest timestamp a task has seen.
A watermark is a guess. Too fast, and late events slip past it; too slow, and one quiet input holds every window open.

A late event is dropped (count the drops), kept by a grace period (which delays every result), or handled by a trigger that answers early and corrects later. The accumulation mode tells the sink whether to add, replace, or take back and apply.
The limit: a stream has no last event, so every final count is a choice of how long to wait. A longer wait gives more complete answers, and later ones.

explain.prompt: A friend's chart of payments per second jumped to 20 times its normal height right after they installed a new version of their counting program. Explain to them why, what to change so it can't happen again, and what new decision that change forces on them.
explain.answer: The chart counted payments by processing time, the moment the program read each one. While the program was stopped for a minute, Kafka kept the new payments. When it came back, it read that backlog at its top speed, 2,000 a second, so those seconds showed 20 times the real rate, after a minute of zeros. People were paying 100 times a second the whole time. The fix is to count by event time, the time the till stamped into each payment, in windows such as one per minute. That forces a new decision: when is a window's count final, since payments can arrive late and out of order? I'd use a watermark, the latest event time seen, and a grace period chosen from the delays I actually measure, say 30 seconds. Payments later than that are dropped and counted, and an alarm watches that count. A rule against stolen cards can't wait for the grace period, so it would read every update as it comes and treat each one as the running total for its window, replacing the one before.

deeper.html:
Percentile watermarks. The Dataflow paper describes watermarks that claim only that, say, 99% of the data before W has arrived. For catching abuse, a fast answer from most of the data beats a complete answer an hour later.

The method names in other engines. In Flink, WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) makes the largest-event-time-minus-5-seconds watermark for each partition, withIdleness marks a quiet input as idle, SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(size, slide) makes what Kafka Streams calls hopping windows, and sideOutputLateData sends late events to a side output. In Spark, withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes") guarantees only that data less than 10 minutes late is not dropped; data later than that may or may not be counted. Lesson 8 covers Spark's output modes.

Watermark alignment. When one Flink source races ahead of another, the step downstream keeps the fast source's events until the slow one's watermark catches up, which can mean a lot of state. Watermark alignment pauses the fast source instead. Flink 2.3 changed it to buffer a few updates (pipeline.watermark-alignment.buffer-size, default 3), so it no longer limits how fast a backlog can be read.

Kafka Streams details. Hopping and tumbling windows include their start, leave out their end and line up with the clock's zero point (1 January 1970); sliding windows include both ends. Window stores keep a day of windows by default. The old window factory methods, which quietly gave every window 24 hours of grace, are deprecated; the ofSizeAndGrace and ofSizeWithNoGrace names make you say what you mean.

Whose clock. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, describes the three-timestamp trick for devices with untrustworthy clocks, in its section on reasoning about time.
